mcqs.question: In the two-stack queue implementation, when does the in-stack-to-out-stack transfer actually happen during a dequeue call?
options: Only when the in-stack has more than one element
Never — enqueue handles the transfer instead
Only when the out-stack is currently empty
mcqs.explanation: The transfer is conditional: dequeue only moves elements from in-stack to out-stack when out-stack has nothing left to pop directly. If out-stack still holds elements, dequeue just pops from it with no transfer at all. Enqueue never transfers anything — it only ever pushes onto in-stack — and the transfer's occurrence has nothing to do with in-stack's element count beyond simply being non-empty.

mcqs.question: Why is the two-stack queue's dequeue operation described as O(1) amortized despite occasionally costing O(n) for a single call?
options: Because O(n) calls never actually occur in practice

Because each element is touched a bounded number of times across its entire lifetime (pushed once, transferred at most once, popped once), so total work over n operations is O(n), averaging to O(1) per call
Because the out-stack is always kept sorted
Because dequeue calls are cached and reused
mcqs.explanation: The amortized argument counts total work across every element's full lifetime rather than any single call in isolation — since each element moves a constant number of times overall, total work for n operations is O(n), which is what "O(1) amortized" means. O(n) calls do occur (whenever the out-stack needs refilling); there's no sorting or caching involved in this structure.

mcqs.question: How does the single-queue-with-rotation stack's cost profile differ from the two-stack queue's, beyond just which operation is expensive?
options: There's no real difference — both are amortized O(1) on their expensive operation
The rotation stack has no expensive operation at all
The two-stack queue is always slower in total than the rotation stack
The rotation stack's expensive push is O(n) on literally every call, with no amortization, while the two-stack queue's expensive dequeue is only occasionally O(n) and amortizes to O(1)
mcqs.explanation: The rotation-based stack rotates its entire queue on every single push, so that cost is paid every time, not amortized away — a genuinely different profile from the two-stack queue, where the expensive transfer happens rarely enough that average cost per call stays O(1). Both structures do have one expensive operation, and neither is universally slower in total — the comparison depends on the actual mix of operations performed.

mcqs.question: Someone analyzes the two-stack queue and reports "dequeue is O(n)" without any further qualification. What's incomplete about that answer?
options: It's fully correct and complete as stated
It's wrong — dequeue is always O(1)
It reports only the worst-case cost for a single call and omits that the amortized cost across a sequence of operations is O(1), which is the actual insight the analysis is testing for
Dequeue's complexity depends on the values being stored, not just the call count
mcqs.explanation: O(n) is a true statement about a single worst-case call, but presenting it alone misses that the total cost across many calls stays linear, meaning the average cost per call is O(1) — the complete, correct answer pairs both numbers. It's not always O(1) per individual call, and the complexity here depends on operation sequence and timing, not on the values stored.
